Overview 
At its roots, our Human Practices involvement comes from  
 
1.​SABPA OC/LA Biochem Forum at UCI 
 
In May, RENATA attended the 18th Annual SABPA OC/LA Biomedical Forum at the Beckman 
Center in Irvine, where Ritvin and Karthik had the opportunity to introduce our early project 
ideas to professionals in biotechnology, healthcare, entrepreneurship, and venture capital. 
Notable participants included Dr. Edward Kim of City of Hope Orange County, Dan Ross of 
BioPharma Capital, Han Li of Riviera Holdings VC, and Benjamin Albaum, co-founder and 
CEO of VIZQ Technologies. We used this opportunity to present RENATA’s preliminary 
progress, pitch SultFlux, and seek perspectives on its potential development in the industry itself. 
 
We wanted to understand what would be required to translate SultFlux, our proposed bacterial 
system for sulfating lithocholic acid (LCA), from an experimental concept into a potentially 
useful healthcare technology. We focused on two dimensions of our project’s potential impact: 
commercial viability and clinical applications. From an investment perspective, we wanted to 
understand what would make SultFlux a feasible biomedical product rather than simply a 
successful laboratory experiment. This meant considering whether our engineered bacterial 
system could consistently sulfate sufficient quantities of lithocholic acid (LCA), whether its 
production and delivery could be scaled economically, and what experimental evidence would be

needed to justify further investment. These questions encouraged us to think about development 
costs, manufacturing, and the practical limitations of bringing a synthetic biology-based product 
to market.  
 
From a clinical perspective, we examined the distinction between demonstrating LCA sulfation 
and establishing a meaningful therapeutic benefit. Although our proposed system aims to modify 
LCA in the gastrointestinal tract, successful enzyme activity alone would not demonstrate that 
the treatment improves patient outcomes. We therefore considered the challenges of safely 
delivering engineered bacteria to the intestine, controlling their activity, evaluating possible 
effects on the broader gut environment, and determining whether the resulting changes in bile 
acid composition could benefit patients experiencing post-cholecystectomy symptoms. 
 
The forum helped us recognize that SultFlux would need to satisfy different standards at each 
stage of development. Our immediate research could establish whether the engineered system 
functions as intended, but clinical translation would require additional evidence of safety and 
therapeutic benefit, while commercialization would depend on scalability, cost, and a viable 
delivery strategy. We incorporated these considerations into our broader evaluation of RENATA's 
future applications, distinguishing what our experiments could demonstrate from what would 
still be required to develop an accessible biomedical treatment. 
 
2.​Interview with Gastroenterologist and Team

To better understand Post-Cholecystectomy Syndrome(PCS) from a professional’s perspective 
and for feedback on our project’s direction, we interviewed Dr. Singh about challenges he’s faced 
around diagnosing and treating patients with gastrointestinal complications following a 
gallbladder removal. One of the first things we discussed was how difficult PCS can be to 
diagnose, due to the fact that symptoms such as diarrhea and bloating often overlap with other 
gastrointestinal conditions such as IBS(Irritable Bowel Syndrome). During our interview, he told 
RENATA that physicians have to consider many possible causes before determining whether a 
patient’s symptoms are related to bile acid metabolism. 
 
Following this, we started to discuss different existing treatments within the medical sphere, such 
as cholestyramine, which patients can take to bind bile acids in the digestive tract. While these 
medications can help patients manage their current symptoms, Dr. Singh explained to us the 
limitations and concerns that patients and physicians have alike when dealing with this treatment. 
Cholestyramine has an unpleasant taste and can interfere with the absorption of other 
medications, as well as how difficult it may be in order to take cholestyramine on a day-to-day 
basis. To RENATA, this meant a lot, as our treatment uses the BtSULT enzyme in order to 
modify secondary bile acids instead of simply binding to them. 
 
Moving on, when we introduced our project, Dr. Singh challenged us to consider whether our 
approach was practical on a realistic scale. He mentioned to us that although digestive symptoms 
may be present after a gallbladder removal on a much wider patient scale, long-term 
complications have a smaller patient base, and many can be treated using existing medications. 
He also encouraged our team to investigate the relationship between the gut microbiome and

other gastrointestinal symptoms, and suggested that focusing only on bile acids may overlook 
other factors that contribute to the discomfort of patients. 
 
This interview helped us think more critically about our project at hand, and made us rethink 
how patients could benefit the most from our treatment and whether our approach could offer a 
meaningful edge over existing medications. 
3.​Interview with Two Patients to Understand Personal 
Experiences 
 
In addition to Dr. Singh and his personal feedback on what PCS entails and how he has seen it 
within the medical environment, we wanted to hear from patients who have experienced or are 
currently experiencing PCS and how that affects their everyday lives. To do this, we conducted 
two individual patient interviews, each revealing different challenges that surround gallbladder 
removal and the possible long-term effects of doing so. 
 
Our first patient had a cholecystectomy in 2009 after having gastrointestinal problems, which 
included pancreatitis and gallbladder dysfunction. After surgery, her digestive symptoms 
continued, which left her with chronic diarrhea and dietary restrictions that she has dealt with for 
over 16 years. She described having to avoid fried food and other dietary triggers, only relying 
on fiber supplements, digestive enzymes, exercise, and strict diet adjustments in order to make 
her symptoms more manageable. One personal account she had was not being able to have 
holiday meals or eat on special occasions, as that could disrupt her routine and worsen her

already-bad symptoms. She explained to us that current medications, including Prilosec, had 
done little to help her. Prilosec is a proton pump inhibitor that stops stomach acid creation at it’s 
origin point. 
 
Our second patient was an elderly Chinese man who shared a different experience than our first. 
Before undergoing his gallbladder removal surgery, he mentioned that he struggled with gas, 
severe bloating, digestive discomfort, and the constant feeling that food was sitting in his chest 
without being digested. Due to this, his appetite and energy were heavily affected. We learned 
that his gallbladder removal cleared up most of his discomfort, but he still struggles with oily and 
fatty foods, particularly those in Chinese cuisine. 
 
Learning Moment: 
 
When we discussed our possible treatment through RENATA, he emphasized to us that an ideal 
medication should be simple to use, especially for older patients. He also expressed concerns 
about long-term side effects from using a medication of this sort. Our first patient also put an 
emphasis on the importance of clinical testing and transparency regarding potential side effects 
or risks of using medication that is biotechnology-based. 
 
4.​Facebook Patient Responses

While our two patient interviews provided valuable insights into patients and how they have 
been affected by gallbladder removals, we realized that our patient base could be significantly 
increased. We realized that we could get insights into PCS from people outside our connections 
or outside of people we emailed or in Orange County.  
 
Thinking about this, we turned to technology. With Facebook communities, we could reach 
people beyond our networks, in other countries and continents. We reached out to people and 
groups in the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and all across the United States in order to 
hear about symptoms or issues post-gallbladder removal.  
 
One unique aspect of our research was the fact that responses varied very significantly. We found 
patients who had pretty seamless surgeries, whereas others had major digestive problems for 
years or decades after surgery. We heard from a patient who experienced malabsorption issues 
for almost 12 years, and another patient mentioned how unpredictable digestive symptoms led to 
them having to organize their days around bathroom visits. One person also mentioned how 
difficult it is to get cholestyramine and this was agreed upon by other responders in the same 
thread.  
 
Overall, our experience with Facebook showed us how technology could contribute to our 
research. By reaching people outside of our community, state, country, and continent, we were 
able to learn about concerns that we might not have identified through our interviews or through 
literature that we read.

Learning Moment: 
These responses made us reconsider how patients would take our treatment. After receiving these 
Facebook responses and going through our research after interviewing patients and professionals 
within the field, we realized that developing an effective enzyme was only one part of the whole. 
For patients, one of the most important part of medicine was how convenient it would be to take 
certain medications to not introduce additional complications along with their already-difficult 
lifestyles.  
 
With this in mind, we moved towards developing a prebiotic-probiotic effect, with the goal of 
minimizing unwanted side effects that other existing medications already had. By shifting, we 
were able to consider how our engineered probiotic would work alongside prebiotic components 
that already existed, and through this we focused less on simply our BtSULT enzyme. The 
patient and professional feedback we received helped us establish convenience and tolerability as 
major factors in our design. 
 
5.​SEVA Collective Event 
 
As a team, we participated in a community service event organized by SEVA Collective, where 
we helped package and distribute food to individuals and families in need. The event brought 
together volunteers from across Orange County, including Santa Ana, Irvine, Tustin, and Costa 
Mesa, which gave us the opportunity to work alongside people from other communities around 
us. All throughout the event, our members spoke to fellow volunteers and families about

RENATA and explained our research into PCS and how our treatment could potentially help 
patients. This event was different from the scientific conferences we attended, as it allowed us to 
discuss our research with people outside of the biotechnology field, which helped us improve our 
presentation skills and make our project easier for people to understand. Outside of simply 
sharing our research, we wanted to put the meaning of “seva”, or selfless service, into practice by 
contributing to the community around us. This also gave us an opportunity to help serve the 
people in need right now, which gave us a reminder about the communities of which our research 
is ultimately going to help to benefit. 
 
 
6.​27th Annual San Diego MedChem Symposium at UCSD

Following all our patient and professional interviews, RENATA travelled to UC San Diego in 
July to attend the 27th Annual San Diego MedChem Symposium. The event brought together 
researchers and pharmaceutical professionals from organizations such as Scripps Research, 
Schrödinger, Novartis, Johnson & Johnson, and Pfizer. At our visit to SABPA in May, we were 
still introducing our initial project ideas, but at this symposium we had the opportunity to 
showcase how far RENATA had progressed throughout the season through multiple project 
iteration points. 
 
By this point we had narrowed our focus to Post-Cholecystectomy Syndrome(PCS) and 
developed our proposed approach of using the custom-engineered BtSULT enzyme to modify 
secondary bile acids. Our Human Practices research had also influenced considerations about 
how patients would need to receive treatment, which is what led us towards opting for a 
prebiotic-probiotic delivery approach to minimize side effects and for ease of use. At UCSD, we 
were able to share this progress with industry professionals and had the opportunity to explain 
how feedback from patients and responses from people suffering from similar issues had shaped 
the direction of our research. 
 
We also took the pleasure in discussing enzyme engineering and the approach we had taken with 
scientists who were quite experienced in small molecule design and drug development, and 
received feedback on parts to consider during the process of creating a custom enzyme, 
specifically enzymatic activity and substrate specificity scores from simulation software we were 
utilizing for our project. These conversations with professionals helped us identify grounds for 
further development and investigation as we continued to work and refine our project. Overall,

this symposium helped RENATA share progress we had made up to that date, allowing us to 
receive industry feedback on the direction of our project, which also gave us the opportunity to 
refine and rethink the way we were engineering our enzyme.

Overview 
We started RENATA from the dream of two high schoolers wanting to bring synthetic biology 
and bioengineering to Orange County, and throughout our journey, we realized just how difficult 
it can be for students to enter the field. Throughout our process of creating this team, we spent 
countless hours pouring over research papers and learned fundamentals of engineering, 
experiencing firsthand how much background knowledge we needed to have before even starting 
to develop our project. 
 
We wanted to change that for other students. After all, we believed that other students deserved 
the same opportunities within science, regardless of how much experience they had with science. 
RENATA started as two high schoolers who shared an interest in biology and wanted to turn that 
curiosity into something tangible and applicable for the people around them. 
 
With this in mind, we developed a few educational initiatives aimed at different age groups and 
levels of scientific understanding. Through our ULP education event, we introduced over 30 
children to DNA and genetics using LEGO Blocks and beads. At Troy High School, we 
organized hands-on biotechnology experiments to demonstrate how microorganisms and 
enzymes work, connecting these concepts to our own research. Finally, we collaborated with 
other iGEM teams to develop an online educational resource for students interested in beginning 
their own journeys in synthetic biology.

Through these initiatives, we hoped to give students something we wished we had when starting 
RENATA: An introduction to synthetic biology that made the subject easier to understand and 
gave them somewhere to begin on their own journey. 
 
1. ULP Education Event: Introducing Children to Genetics 
Bringing DNA into the Classroom 
For our first education initiative, RENATA worked with ULP to introduce over 30 children ages 
nine and above to the fundamentals of DNA, genetics, and synthetic biology overall.  
 
To us, teaching synthetic biology presented us with quite an interesting question. How do you 
explain a molecule that can’t be seen with the naked eye to a student who might never have 
studied cells before? 
 
We began to tackle this problem by introducing DNA as a set of instructions that organisms use 
in order to develop and function. Furthering this, we introduced the relationship between DNA 
and observable characteristics. Traits such as hair texture and certain inherited physical features 
such as height helped provide some familiar examples for how genetic information can influence 
and come to create an organism as a whole. Through this, our students were given something that 
they already understood before we introduced more unfamiliar concepts 
 
From there, we explained the basic idea behind synthetic biology. Scientists can study genetic 
information, and through processes within genetic engineering, modify certain sequences to

change how an organism functions. This is a similar principle behind many iGEM projects, 
including RENATA’s work.  
 
However, we wanted students not only to listen and see these ideas, but also experience them 
tangibly instead of simply relying on verbal explanations. With this in mind, we designed two 
activities that turned genetic concepts into a tangible model that students could experience in 
front of them. 
 
Activity 1: Building DNA using LEGO Bricks 
 
Our first activity used LEGO blocks to represent the four kinds of nucleotide bases that make up 
DNA. Each DNA base was represented by a different type of color of block, which allowed 
students to distinguish between adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine. Students could then 
arrange the blocks into sequences, which created a simplified physical representation of genetic 
information.

The purpose of this activity was to explain why the order of DNA bases matters. Two sequences 
can contain the same bases but result in unique genetic information being stored, as those bases 
are organized differently. By rearranging their LEGO bricks, students could see that the sequence 
itself was important even when the building materials were the same. 
 
We connected this idea to the way genetic changes can influence an organism’s traits. In real 
biological systems, certain sequences of DNA contain instructions for making proteins. Proteins 
perform many of the functions necessary for life, and changes to the sequences encoding them 
can sometimes change their structure or activity.

This also gave us a way to introduce genetic engineering without beginning with unfamiliar 
laboratory techniques. If genetic information is stored in sequences, scientists can modify 
biological functions by changing those sequences to their liking. Although the LEGO model 
simplified the actual complexity of DNA, it gave students a starting point for understanding how 
genetic information can be modified. 
 
All in all, this activity allowed students to experiment with different arrangements themselves, 
which allowed them to directly work with the model, compare their own sequences, and ask 
questions about how those changes may affect a living organism on a long term scale. 
 
Activity 2: Exploring DNA Traits Through Beads 
 
Our second activity was centered around defining the relationship between genetics and physical 
characteristics that an organism has. We developed a trait chart that students could use to identify 
some of their own physical characteristics. Different colored beads corresponded to different 
responses on the chart, hence allowing students to create a physical representation of their 
selected traits. This gave a look into how inherited genetic information can relate to observable 
physical characteristics, which is a little different from the LEGO activity we had done 
previously.  
 
Students used their completed bead arrangements to compare traits that they had recorded down 
from their own personal perspectives. This also helped introduce the concept of variation 
between individuals and why members of the same species can have different physical

characteristics. Additionally, this activity created opportunities to discuss inheritance and the 
relationship between genes and traits. We introduced these ideas through simplified examples 
appropriate for the students' ages, since many physical characteristics are influenced by multiple 
genes and environmental factors. 
 
When designing this activity, one of the main considerations that we put into picture was to make 
science personal enough for students to understand. DNA is quite an abstract concept when 
understood as a double helix or sequence of nucleotides. However, when students are able to see 
their own characteristics, it gives students a familiar example of why genetic information 
matters.

Educational Purpose and Synthetic Biology Connection 
After introducing DNA sequences and inherited traits, we connected the two activities to the 
basic principles of synthetic biology. The LEGO activity showed students how genetic 
information is organized, while the bead activity gave them examples of how biological 
characteristics can vary. Together, they provided a base for explaining to younger individuals 
how scientists study genetic information and attempt to modify biological systems. 
Our ULP event was designed as an introduction to genetics for students who had limited 
experience with molecular biology. We taught over 30 children through activities that allowed 
them to build models, examine their own characteristics, and discuss the concepts behind their 
work. The LEGO and bead activities were selected because they made different parts of genetics 
easier to visualize. One dealt with the information stored in DNA, while the other dealt with 
observable characteristics influenced by genetics. These activities also gave us experience 
explaining scientific concepts without relying on the terminology we normally use when 
discussing our project.  
 
2. Butterfly Project Collaboration 
 
As part of RENATA’s education initiatives, we collaborated with the Butterfly Project in order to 
organize an interactive workshop for students in grades 3-6. Our goal was to introduce the major 
topic of DNA to younger students, while comparing it to other examples of how living organisms 
function. Since our project involves genetically engineering bacteria to produce an enzyme that 
modifies bile acids, we wanted to help younger students understand the basic science that makes

this possible, to one day bring students closer to the sphere of synthetic biology. Rather than 
immediately defining what DNA was, we compared DNA to a recipe book that contains 
instructions that tell cells how to grow and function.  
 
One of the main activities was the hands-on strawberry DNA extraction experiment that the 
students partook in. Students worked in small groups to extract and observe DNA from 
strawberries, which allowed them to see the genetic material we had discussed during the 
presentation. We also introduced a genetics interactive activity, in which students were able to 
use randomly assigned characteristics to design a fictional person, which helped them understand 
how genetic information can influence physical traits. These activities all helped students acquire 
foundations of genetic engineering in a way that was accessible to elementary school students.  
 
This workshop also allowed us to connect our educational initiatives to RENATA’s main mission 
of making synthetic biology more accessible to kids all around Southern California. The same 
basic principles that we introduced to the kids at Butterfly Project are central to our own project. 
Even though our project involves the use of much more complex genetic engineering techniques, 
we wanted students to understand that biotechnology starts with the same concepts that they 
learned in our workshops. By introducing these ideas at a younger age, we hoped to encourage 
students to pursue and explore biology and biotechnology for their futures.

3. Troy Biotechnology Education Day 
Bringing Biotechnology into the High School Classroom 
After our education event at ULP, we wanted to move towards a more complex and experimental 
side of explaining synthetic biology and our project. Our event at Troy High School gave the 
opportunity for students to see how living organisms function through hands-on experiments. 
 
Our event was comprised of three experimental stations, each of them focusing on a different 
biological process involved in synthetic biology. Karthik prepared most of the experimental 
setups, and Humza led a presentation that introduced concepts behind the activities that the 
participants would do. Our idea for the event was that students would move between the 
presentation and experiments, learning about a particular concept before visiting the 
corresponding station. After each activity, we returned to the presentation to explain the 
significance and relevance to biotechnology and RENATA’s project goals. 
 
Part of our presentation was also an introduction to the research that RENATA partook in 
throughout the season. Our presentation covered the role of bile acids in digestion, the BtSULT 
enzyme we were engineering to modify secondary bile acids, and our proposed use of probiotic 
bacteria as a delivery system.

Activity 1: Observing Bacteria Under a Microscope 
 
Our first station introduced students to microorganisms through yogurt. We prepared samples of 
plain yogurt and milk for students to examine under microscopes, which allowed them to 
compare the two and get a look into how bacteria affect and influence fermentation.  
 
During this activity, we also discussed the importance of using controls within experiments. 
Comparing the yogurt sample with milk gave students a reference point for interpreting what 
they observed. We taught the lesson of needing evidence to see an observed difference, which is 
an important lesson when doing any sort of biological research. 
 
We selected this experiment because bacteria are central to RENATA's proposed treatment. Our 
project involves engineering probiotic bacteria, and yogurt provided students with a recognizable 
example of microorganisms that performed useful biological functions. From there, we could 
explain how synthetic biologists take advantage of these natural capabilities and engineer

bacteria to perform additional functions, including those with potential medical applications, as 
explained in the presentation. 
 
Activity 2: Yeast Balloon Experiment 
 
Our second activity gave a look into how microorganisms respond to different nutrients. We 
showed this through a yeast fermentation experiment. After preparing containers with varying 
types and amounts of sugar, students were able to see how yeast produced carbon dioxide that 
inflated balloons attached to each container. By comparing balloons, students were able to see 
how changes in nutrient availability affected fermentation.  
 
We connected this experiment to RENATA’s proposed probiotic treatment, and explained how 
engineered bacteria depend on their surrounding environment in order to function effectively. In 
the same way that the yeast responded to different available nutrients, our engineered bacteria 
would need to operate under the conditions of the gastrointestinal tract.  
 
Activity 3: Investigating Enzyme Activity Through Foam 
 
Our final station focused on enzymes, which is the same biological component that most directly 
relates to RENATA’s research. We tried to show the activity of catalase, and by capturing 
released oxygen in soap bubbles, we created a visible reaction that students could observe and 
compare across multiple experimental conditions.

We used varying amounts of hydrogen peroxide to demonstrate how the concentration of a 
substrate can influence enzyme activity. Students observed the foam produced by the reactions, 
and we discussed why increasing the amount of substrate can initially increase reaction activity 
but eventually reaches a point where another factor becomes limiting. We also included a control 
to demonstrate the importance of having the correct substrate available for an enzyme to perform 
its function. 
 
The catalase experiment gave students a way to understand these ideas through an observable 
reaction. They could see how changing experimental conditions affected the output of an 
enzyme, providing context for why RENATA needed to evaluate its own enzyme designs 
carefully. The foam experiment used a different enzyme and reaction from our project, but the 
underlying questions about enzyme activity were closely related to the work we were 
conducting. 
 
Takeaway and Connection: 
 
Through our three experimental stations, we wanted students to understand how different 
biological processes come together in synthetic biology research. The yogurt experiment 
explained microorganisms and their useful functions, the yeast balloon experiment demonstrated 
how environmental conditions can affect microbial activity, and the catalase experiment explored 
the role of enzymes in chemical reactions. By alternating between presentation and the 
experimental stations, students could observe the biological principles behind our research and 
understand how they apply to an actual biotechnology project. Through this event, we hoped to

make synthetic biology more accessible to our school's students and give them a firsthand look at 
the scientific concepts and experimental reasoning involved in developing RENATA.

4. Biotech Youth Literacy Directive Club 
Karthik and Humza founded the Biotechnology Youth Literacy Directive (BYLD), a student-led 
club dedicated to introducing biotechnology and synthetic biology to students at our school. 
Through multiple lectures on DNA analysis techniques and their applications in research, we 
helped students explore concepts beyond their regular biology classes. BYLD also served as a 
pathway into RENATA, encouraging students interested in biotechnology to get involved in 
iGEM and participate in hands-on synthetic biology research. 
 
 
5. iGEM Guide Collaboration

In collaboration with iGEM teams NBJF and DBHS-CA, RENATA contributed to a larger 
open-source education initiative designed to help new iGEMmers establish their own iGEM 
teams. Humza drew from the challenges we faced as a team in our first year and created the 
guide “Beginner's Guide to High School iGEM: Research Fundamentals”, compiling the 
scientific knowledge he wished he had when co-founding our team. 
 
The guide introduces viewers to the fundamentals of synthetic biology, covering DNA, proteins, 
the DBTL cycle, genetic circuit design, gene regulation, plasmids, and DNA assembly 
techniques such as Golden Gate Assembly. Also, it provides diagrams and references to 
additional research resources, which help students understand how these concepts apply to actual 
work in the laboratory. We wanted this collaboration to be a way for us to help make the early 
stages of synthetic biology less overwhelming, which gives future iGEM teams an accessible 
point to start their journey without requiring them to piece together hundreds of hours of 
foundational knowledge that we had to learn independently!
